blobs.reading: Linear search checks each element in a list, one at a time, until it finds the target or reaches the end. It always works, regardless of whether the list is sorted, but in the worst case it looks at every element.

exercise.prompt: Implement linear_search(items, target) returning the index of target in items, or -1 if not found.
exercise.test_code:
from solution import linear_search
assert linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 8) == 2
assert linear_search([5, 3, 8, 1], 9) == -1
assert linear_search([], 1) == -1
print('ok')
hints: You need to look at each element in order, comparing it to target.
Use enumerate(items) to get both the index and value as you loop.
Return i as soon as items[i] == target; if the loop finishes, return -1.

extra_questions.prompt: Implement count_occurrences(items, target) returning how many times target appears in items.
extra_questions.test_code:
from solution import count_occurrences
assert count_occurrences([5, 3, 8, 3, 3], 3) == 3
assert count_occurrences([5, 3, 8], 9) == 0
print('ok')
hints: Walk the list once, same as linear_search, but keep counting instead of returning early.
extra_questions.reference_solution:
def count_occurrences(items, target):
    return sum(1 for value in items if value == target)

extra_questions.prompt: Why is linear search's worst-case time still O(n) even though it sometimes finds the target on the very first comparison?
extra_questions.expected_answer: Worst-case describes the bound over all possible inputs, not a typical run - if the target is absent or happens to be last, linear search must check every element, so the bound that holds for every possible input is O(n); an occasional early find doesn't change what the worst case requires.

blobs.reading: Binary search only works on a sorted list. It repeatedly halves the search range: compare the target to the middle element, and discard the half that cannot contain it. This is why it beats linear search on large sorted lists - each step eliminates half the remaining candidates.

exercise.prompt: Implement binary_search(items, target) for a sorted list, returning the index of target or -1 if not found.
exercise.test_code:
from solution import binary_search
assert binary_search([1, 3, 5, 8, 9], 8) == 3
assert binary_search([1, 3, 5, 8, 9], 2) == -1
assert binary_search([], 1) == -1
print('ok')
hints: Track a low and high boundary and look at the midpoint between them.
If items[mid] == target you're done; otherwise narrow low or high based on the comparison.
low = 0, high = len(items) - 1; while low <= high: mid = (low + high) // 2 ...

blobs.concept: Why binary search needs sorted input
blobs.reading: Binary search's correctness depends entirely on the list being sorted: discarding half the range is only valid because a sorted order guarantees the target can't be in the discarded half. On unsorted data the algorithm can silently return the wrong answer instead of failing loudly.

exercise.prompt: Given an unsorted list, why might binary_search return -1 or a wrong index even when the target is present? Answer in your own words before revealing.
exercise.expected_answer: Because binary search's halving step assumes elements to one side of the midpoint are all smaller (or larger); on unsorted data that assumption doesn't hold, so it can discard the half that actually contains the target, causing it to miss a present value or return an incorrect index.
